# delayedBahn — error404.ai Share your train trip, and delayedBahn tells you how late each train is likely to be and whether you will make your change. It learns from Deutsche Bahn's own timetable and delay data. Built by team error404.ai at the European Hackathon League Zurich. ![Demo](docs/images/demo.png) ## Contents 1. [Problem](#problem) 2. [What we built](#what-we-built) 3. [The app](#the-app) 4. [Data sources](#data-sources) 5. [What the DB data solves](#what-the-db-data-solves) 6. [Architecture](#architecture) 7. [Model](#model) 8. [Code structure](#code-structure) 9. [Quickstart](#quickstart) 10. [Team](#team) 11. [Built with](#built-with) 12. [Screenshots](#screenshots) --- ## Problem - The DB app shows the planned journey, not the chance that it actually works. - A trip with a change fails at its tightest connection, and travellers only find out on the platform. - Delays are uneven: most trains are a few minutes late, a few are very late. A single "expected delay" hides the risk. ## What we built - **Share a trip** from the DB app into our web app. It reads the trains, stations and times. - **Get a forecast per train**: likely arrival delay, a range, and the chance of making each change. - **Get advice**: the plan is fine, add buffer, or take an earlier or later connection. ## The app - **Start screen:** paste the text you copied from the DB app, or share it straight from your phone. The app can be installed on your home screen. - **Map:** your route drawn on a map of Germany, with the trains moving along it. - **Train cards:** one card per train with the likely delay, the range, and a short explanation from the model. - **Advice:** a clear verdict for the whole trip, and other options if a change looks tight. --- ## Data sources All product data comes from Deutsche Bahn's official API Marketplace. | API | What we use it for | Endpoints | Coverage | Auth | |---|---|---|---|---| | [Timetables](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/timetables) | Planned stops, live delays, cancellations, platform changes, route of every train | `station/{name}`, `plan/{eva}/{date}/{hour}`, `fchg/{eva}` | Current and upcoming trains | `DB_CLIENT_ID`, `DB_API_KEY` (free plan) | | [RIS::Stations](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/ris-stations) | Official station names and EVA numbers | `stop-places/by-key` | Current | Same keys | Both APIs are called with the headers `DB-Client-Id` and `DB-Api-Key` (`scripts/db_timetables.py`, `scripts/db_live_extract.py`). The history used for training are stored responses from the same Timetables feeds, in one row per train per stop, published as [`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data). ## What the DB data solves | Traveller problem | DB data that answers it | |---|---| | "Which train and station is this?" | Timetables `station` lookup and RIS::Stations turn names from the share text into exact EVA station IDs | | "Is my train late right now?" | The Timetables change feed (`fchg`) gives the current delay at every stop the train has passed | | "Will it get worse before my stop?" | Planned route (`ppth`) and stops ahead, plus how earlier trains on the same line did today | | "Is this station having a bad day?" | Late share across all trains at the station recently | | "Will this train be cancelled?" | Cancellation flags in the change feed, and how often this route was cancelled before | | "Will I make my change?" | Planned arrival and departure times of both trains, combined with both delay forecasts | --- ## Architecture ```mermaid graph TD A["Live DB data
today's delays from Timetables + RIS::Stations"] --> C["Delay model
fine-tuned Llama 3.2 3B"] B["Past DB data
past delays, every train, every stop"] --> C C --> D["Web app
shared trip in, forecast out"] ``` 1. **Collect:** we read timetables and delays from the DB APIs. 2. **Learn:** the model learns how delays grow along a trip from past records. 3. **Predict:** when you share a trip, the app sends it to the model together with today's live delays and shows you the forecast. ## Model - **Base model:** Llama 3.2 3B (`unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B`), extended with [OpenTSLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02410) so it can read time series next to text. Starts from the `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` checkpoint and is fine-tuned with LoRA. - **Training data:** past DB stop records, turned into training examples. Each example is one train and one stop it is heading to. - **Input:** for one train and one target stop, the delays so far on this trip, how earlier trains to that stop did, and the recent lateness of the station, as numbers and one short sentence. - **Output:** `Answer: ` or `Answer: cancelled`. From this we read the most likely delay, a range, and the chance of cancellation. - **Connections:** the chance of making a change comes from the two trains' forecasts and the planned transfer time (`trip/connection.py`). - **Training:** fine-tuned on Nebius GPUs. Full commands are in `app/agents/src/features/db_delay/trip/README.md`. --- ## Code structure ``` api/ Vercel entry: sends /api/* to the backend app/backend/ Node API (no dependencies): parse share text, predict, recommend app/frontend/ React web app: paste or share a trip, forecast, advice, map app/agents/ Python: data building, model training, model server src/features/db_delay/trip/ the delay model (build, train, serve) src/features/db_route/ route-level delay experiments scripts/ DB Timetables and RIS::Stations clients team-setup/ team coordination: tasks, decisions, hooks bootstrap.sh local setup check ``` | File | What it does | |---|---| | `scripts/db_live_extract.py` | Calls Timetables and RIS::Stations, merges plan and changes into one row per train per stop | | `scripts/db_timetables.py` | Prints the next departures and delays for a station | | `app/backend/src/features/share-parser/grammar.js` | Reads DB share text into a journey (`POST /api/journeys/parse`) | | `app/backend/src/features/delay-prediction/routes/delay-prediction.js` | Asks the model for each train, works out change risk (`POST /api/predict`) | | `app/backend/src/features/recommendation/routes/recommendation.js` | Gives the verdict and alternatives (`POST /api/recommend`) | | `app/agents/src/features/db_delay/trip/build.py` | Turns stop records into training examples | | `app/agents/src/features/db_delay/trip/train.py` | Fine-tunes the model | | `app/agents/src/features/db_delay/trip/serve.py` | Serves forecasts to the backend, using live Timetables data | --- ## Quickstart ```bash git clone https://github.com/KiraKami-dev/temporal_ai_error404.ai.git cd temporal_ai_error404.ai cp .env.example .env # add DB_CLIENT_ID and DB_API_KEY from developers.deutschebahn.com ln -s ../../.env app/backend/.env python3 scripts/db_timetables.py "Hamburg Hbf" # live departures from DB cd app/backend && npm run dev # terminal 1: API on http://localhost:8000 npm --prefix app/frontend ci && npm --prefix app/frontend run dev # terminal 2, repo root: app on http://127.0.0.1:5173 ``` To run the trained model locally, see "Model files (required)" in `app/agents/src/features/db_delay/trip/README.md`. ## Team error404.ai — Akshat Khair, Gaurav Kulkarni, Jonas (`josteng`), Yash (`yash-epte`) ## Built with - European Hackathon League Zurich - Deutsche Bahn API Marketplace: [Timetables](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/timetables), [RIS::Stations](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/ris-stations) - [OpenTSLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02410), Llama 3.2, Nebius GPUs --- ## Screenshots ![App](docs/images/demo.png) ![Data extraction code](docs/images/code_data.png) ![Model training code](docs/images/code_model.png) ![Example run](docs/images/example.png) === app/README.md # app/ The actual product. Everything under `../team-setup/` is coordination, not code — this is where the hackathon build lives. - **`frontend/`** — whatever UI framework this event's stack picks. - **`backend/`** — whatever backend language/framework this event's stack picks. - **`agents/`** — the AI/agent pipeline layer (detection, RAG, whatever the challenge needs). - **`shared/`** — generated from `../team-setup/state/03-contract-freeze/contract.md`. Never hand-edited — see `shared/README.md`. Inside each of `frontend/`, `backend/`, `agents/`: one folder per feature under `src/features/`, not a `components/`/`routes/`/`models/` split at the top level. Copy `src/features/_TEMPLATE/` to start a new feature. Feature names should match 1:1 across layers where a feature spans them (e.g. `frontend/src/features//` and `backend/src/features//` are the same feature, two halves). Who owns which folder is decided fresh per event and lives only in `../team-setup/state/owners.md` — not here, and not fixed by this template. ## Running everything together Backend is Node ≥ 22 with zero dependencies; frontend and agents stacks are still placeholders. Current run commands: ```bash (cd app/backend && npm run dev) & # http://localhost:8000/api/health cd app/backend && npm run train -- doctor # Nebius GPU training setup check ``` The fine-tuned trip-delay model runs locally with its own script, which also starts the backend and the PWA. It needs model files that are not in Git: see "Model files (required)" in `agents/src/features/db_delay/trip/README.md`. ```bash app/agents/src/features/db_delay/trip/run_local.sh start # model on :8502, app on http://localhost:8000 ``` GPU training runs on Nebius Serverless AI jobs via `backend/src/features/training-jobs/` (see its README). Once the other folders have real dependencies filled in, extend this — e.g.: ```bash # example once a Next.js + FastAPI + Python-agents stack is chosen: (cd app/frontend && npm run dev) & (cd app/backend && npm run dev) & (cd app/agents && python -m agents.main) & ``` `bootstrap.sh` detects whatever is actually in these three folders and installs dependencies accordingly — it never assumes a stack.

--- app/agents/src/features/db_route/discover/README.md
# Agentic data retrieval for the db-route datasets

A search, assess, select, retrieve and validate loop for open time-series sources, with an
LLM agent proposing and deterministic code disposing. It produced the source decisions behind
the `error404/db-route-*` TimeNet connectors; the run of record is committed under `results/`.

## What the agent decides and what the code verifies

| step | the agent (gpt-4o-mini, JSON mode, `llm.py`) proposes | the code verifies or refuses |
|---|---|---|
| search | registry queries for the four catalogues, from the data spec | every query is run against the live registry API (`scout.py`) |
| assess | relevance of each candidate to the spec, with a reason | licence allow-list, credentials, coverage window and cadence gates (`gates.py`), cheapest first |
| select | rubric fields per surviving source (`rubric.py`) | a live probe: DuckDB over HTTP range reads measures rows, columns, coverage and the 2025-11-02 station-basis step (`probe.py`) |
| retrieve | a column map from the source schema to the spec's fields | `verify_schema()`: every named column must exist and type-check against the probe, or the map is rejected |
| validate | | the accept/reject table is written as `REJECTIONS.md` with the failing gate per source |

An unverifiable proposal is dropped, never negotiated. Every LLM call, its prompt and its
answer are logged to `results/agent_log.json` so a reader can audit each decision.

## Run it

```bash
cd app/agents/src/features/db_route
OPENAI_API_KEY=...  python -m discover.run --out results     # with the agent
python -m discover.run --out results                         # without: the same gates and probes, no proposals
```

Standard library only, plus `duckdb` for the live probes. Without `OPENAI_API_KEY` the loop
still runs and records that no agent was present.

## Run of record (`results/`)

Window 2025-11-02 to 2026-08-31, four registries (a known list, HuggingFace datasets, govdata
CKAN, Zenodo): 354 candidates, 18 passed every gate, 7 of those probed live and used, 11
accepted on metadata only and left as candidates. The rest are rejected with the gate that
failed in `REJECTIONS.md`. `assessment.json` carries every entry with its gate result, probe
measurements, rubric, agent verdict and verified schema map; `candidates.jsonl` is the raw
scout output.

The code is self-contained: nothing here imports from the rest of `db_route`. The connectors
consume its decisions, not its code.

=== db_route RESULTS
# Results: the S/M/L/XM bake-off on all-Germany data

2,000 steps, batch 8, `plain_crps`, seed 0, one H100 per profile (`train_route.py`, jobs `route-2k-*-v3`, 13 Sep 2026 02:50–03:58 UTC).
Median error / CRPS in minutes on the departure-delay task, 600 scored rows per cell (all rows where a cell is smaller).
GBM = scikit-learn histogram gradient boosting on the same information (per-series mean/std/last/max + scalar annotations), quantile heads for CRPS.
Persistence = the context mean of the entity's own delay series (this service at this station where the profile carries it, else this service group), a point forecast. Route history = the empirical quantiles of that same series.
Blend = one weight on the TSLM quantiles fitted on `val` by CRPS. Classification = generated-answer accuracy on 64 rows (late/on-time and cause family together) vs the majority class.

## Reading

- **At 2k steps nobody is far from persistence.** On unseen trains the TSLM beats the entity's own context mean by 0.00–0.08 min and the GBM by 0.04–0.16; the distributional route-history baseline is clearly worse (its quantiles are too wide). The 12k grid is the test of whether training longer opens a real gap; the seed runs give its noise floor.

- **Quarter (6 h × 60 d) wins every cell.** Lowest error on both held-out cells and the smallest seen→unseen gap (0.13 min); week (7 d hourly) memorises — 0.6 min worse on unseen trains than on seen ones.
- **Multiscale does not add.** The plan's additivity question (does long history help *on top of* the week?) gets a no at this budget: second-worst on every cell. Caveat: it carries 2.8× the encoder tokens of the others and saw the identical 16k samples, so a fixed step budget under-trains the largest input.
- **The TSLM ties the tabular baseline on unseen trains** (quarter/test: 1.820 vs 1.816, CRPS 1.370 vs 1.374) and trails it by ~0.08 min on seen trains at 2k steps — the regime the literature predicts (RIDE: XGBoost within 4% of the best deep model) and what the trip-delay work found before its 12k-step runs.
- **The blend is the best forecast on every cell**, and the TSLM's fitted share rises with profile quality: 0.15 (week) → 0.20 (season) → 0.30 (quarter).
- **Publish `test` (unseen trains and weeks) as the headline and the gap to `test_seen_entity` as the memorisation estimate.** `test_seen_time` is optimistic by construction and is reported, not headlined.
- Everything is ~30% under the naive train-median baseline; 10–90% coverage sits at 0.70–0.80 against a 0.80 target, so the distributions are slightly narrow.

Artifacts: `s3://error404-db-route/runs/route-2k/<profile>/{metrics.json, checkpoint.pt, scalar_<cell>.npz}`; local baselines/blend in `baselines_local.json` beside them.

| multiscale | test | 506 | 2.43 / 1.87 | 2.36 / 1.83 | 2.51 | 3.06 / 2.21 | 2.33 / 1.83 (0.00) | 3.07 | 0.62 / 0.41 |
| multiscale | test_seen_time | 600 | 1.90 / 1.46 | 1.73 / 1.36 | 2.27 | 2.75 / 2.00 | 1.73 / 1.36 (0.00) | 2.70 | 0.64 / 0.38 |

## Reading

- **At 2k steps nobody is far from persistence.** On unseen trains the TSLM beats the entity's own context mean by 0.00–0.08 min and the GBM by 0.04–0.16; the distributional route-history baseline is clearly worse (its quantiles are too wide). The 12k grid is the test of whether training longer opens a real gap; the seed runs give its noise floor.

- **Quarter (6 h × 60 d) wins every cell.** Lowest error on both held-out cells and the smallest seen→unseen gap (0.13 min); week (7 d hourly) memorises — 0.6 min worse on unseen trains than on seen ones.
- **Multiscale does not add.** The plan's additivity question (does long history help *on top of* the week?) gets a no at this budget: second-worst on every cell. Caveat: it carries 2.8× the encoder tokens of the others and saw the identical 16k samples, so a fixed step budget under-trains the largest input.
- **The TSLM ties the tabular baseline on unseen trains** (quarter/test: 1.820 vs 1.816, CRPS 1.370 vs 1.374) and trails it by ~0.08 min on seen trains at 2k steps — the regime the literature predicts (RIDE: XGBoost within 4% of the best deep model) and what the trip-delay work found before its 12k-step runs.
- **The blend is the best forecast on every cell**, and the TSLM's fitted share rises with profile quality: 0.15 (week) → 0.20 (season) → 0.30 (quarter).
- **Publish `test` (unseen trains and weeks) as the headline and the gap to `test_seen_entity` as the memorisation estimate.** `test_seen_time` is optimistic by construction and is reported, not headlined.
- Everything is ~30% under the naive train-median baseline; 10–90% coverage sits at 0.70–0.80 against a 0.80 target, so the distributions are slightly narrow.

Artifacts: `s3://error404-db-route/runs/route-2k/<profile>/{metrics.json, checkpoint.pt, scalar_<cell>.npz}`; local baselines/blend in `baselines_local.json` beside them.

# delayedBahn — error404.ai Share your train trip from the DB app, and delayedBahn tells you how late each train is likely to be, whether you will make your change, and what to do about it. Two fine-tuned time-series language models, trained on Deutsche Bahn's own delay history, answer every trip you share. Built by team error404.ai at the European Hackathon League Zurich. ![Demo](docs/images/demo.png) ## Contents 1. [The problem](#the-problem) 2. [What we built](#what-we-built) 3. [Features, screen by screen](#features-screen-by-screen) 4. [How a shared trip flows through the system](#how-a-shared-trip-flows-through-the-system) 5. [Architecture](#architecture) 6. [Data: sources and the agentic retrieval loop](#data-sources-and-the-agentic-retrieval-loop) 7. [The two models and why we combine them](#the-two-models-and-why-we-combine-them) 8. [Numbers](#numbers) 9. [What is honest to say and what is not](#what-is-honest-to-say-and-what-is-not) 10. [Code structure](#code-structure) 11. [Quickstart](#quickstart) 12. [Team](#team) 13. [Built with](#built-with) 14. [Screenshots](#screenshots) --- ## The problem Deutsche Bahn runs about 40,000 trains a day, and every traveller knows the feeling: the planned journey looks fine on paper, then the first train arrives eleven minutes late and the change at Donauwörth is gone. The DB app shows the plan. It does not show the chance that the plan works. We cannot make the trains run on time. We can give travellers a reliable and comfortable journey anyway: know in advance which change is at risk, how much buffer would fix it, and which alternative to take if it fails. Three things make this hard, and shape everything below: - **Delays are uneven.** Most trains are a few minutes late, a few are very late. A single "expected delay" hides the risk; what a traveller needs is a distribution and the chance of the tight change. - **A journey is a chain.** It fails at its tightest connection. Per-train forecasts have to be chained across transfers. - **Data lives in many places.** Live positions from the DB API, months of history in open datasets, station cause codes, cancellations. Deciding what to fetch and what to drop is a task in itself. ## What we built - **Share a trip** from the DB app straight into our installable web app. It reads the trains, stations and times from the share text. - **A forecast per train:** likely arrival delay, a 10 to 90% range, the chance of arriving on time, and the chance of making each change, chained across the whole journey. - **Advice:** the plan is fine, add this much buffer, leave home by this time, or take one of these alternatives. If you already missed a change, the next connections from where you stand, each scored. - **The model's own words:** for every train, first the exact inputs the model read, then the explanation it writes itself. - **Why:** what usually goes wrong at each station, from DB's cause codes. - **Two models that complement each other:** a trip model that reads today's live train position, and a route model that knows every recorded service at every station. The backend asks the second whenever the first has nothing to go on. - **An agentic data retrieval loop** that searched four open-data registries, assessed 354 candidate sources, and kept the 7 that survived licence, coverage and live schema checks. Every decision is logged and auditable. ## Features, screen by screen | Screen | What it does | Backend call | |---|---|---| | **Plan** | Paste or share DB text. Drop a `.txt`. Try the example trip. Journey cards per train. | `POST /api/journeys/parse` | | **Map** | Your route on a satellite globe of Germany, legs coloured by risk, trains moving along the track, camera choreography per screen. | none | | **My journey** | Headline: the chance your plan fails. Per-train delay bars with range, chain strip across changes, a buffer slider that re-runs the chain on the client. Each train card carries the model's take: instantly the exact inputs it read, then its freely written explanation when ready, with a live "writing, train 2 of 3" note. | `POST /api/predict`, `POST /api/explain` | | **What next?** | Verdict and advice, leave-home-by time, alternatives compared, "I missed my connection" re-route list drawn on the map, share the result. | `POST /api/recommend`, `POST /api/reroute` | | **Why?** | Cause families at the station (works, weather, technical, knock-on), top DB cause codes, a 7-day sparkline. | `GET /api/causes` | | **Evidence** | Data sourcing, the model-versus-baseline chart, limitations, install button. | none | | **Install and share** | Installable PWA with a Web Share Target, so "Share" in DB Navigator lists delayedBahn. Stage mode for presenting from the app. | `GET /api/seed/demo` | Everything the app shows is labelled by where it came from: live forecast, recorded history, class average, or illustrative example. It never substitutes sample data for a real trip. ## How a shared trip flows through the system ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant DB as DB Navigator participant App as delayedBahn PWA participant BE as Node backend :8000 participant Trip as Trip model :8502
(Llama 3.2 3B + OpenTSLM, live DB data) participant Route as Route model :8501/:8503
(Llama 3.2 3B + OpenTSLM, 60-day history) participant DBAPI as DB Timetables API DB->>App: share text (Web Share Target /share?text=) App->>BE: POST /api/journeys/parse BE-->>App: Journey (trains, EVA stations, times) App->>BE: POST /api/predict BE->>Trip: forecast every leg Trip->>DBAPI: live position, stops ahead, station lateness Trip-->>BE: minute distribution per leg, or "class average" when no trip matches BE->>Route: forecast only the legs the trip model could not Route-->>BE: distribution from the recorded service at that station BE-->>App: chained forecast: per-train delay, change risk, plan-fail probability App->>BE: POST /api/recommend BE-->>App: verdict, buffer, alternatives loop one train at a time App->>BE: POST /api/explain BE->>Trip: generate the rationale in the model's own words Trip-->>App: two-sentence summary + full text end ``` 1. **Parse.** A grammar reads the DB share text in German or English (`RE16 (59129) … From 16:39 Nürnberg Hbf, Platform 5`) into trains, stations and times, and resolves stations to EVA numbers. 2. **Forecast.** The trip model gets every leg. For a train it can find in the live timetable it reads the delay so far, the stops ahead, how earlier trains on the line did today and how late the station is running, and answers with a probability for every minute from 0 to 999 plus the chance of cancellation. 3. **Complement.** For legs where the trip model has no recorded or live trip and would only return the average of its train class, the backend sends exactly those legs to the route model, which forecasts the recorded service at that station from 60 days of six-hourly history. The reply names both models and marks which legs came from which. 4. **Chain.** The change probability at each transfer comes from the two trains' distributions and the planned transfer time; the plan-fail probability chains all changes. This is a JavaScript port of the Python `connection.py`, so the buffer slider can re-run it on the client. 5. **Advise.** The recommendation feature turns the chain into a verdict, a leave-home-by time, and scored alternatives. 6. **Explain.** After the forecast, the app asks for each train's explanation in turn. Generation is slow on a laptop, about a minute per train, so the card shows the instant rationale first and swaps in the model's own words when they arrive. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Data["Data layer (Python, app/agents)"] R["Agentic retrieval loop
search · assess · select · retrieve · validate
LLM proposes, code verifies"] H["piebro/deutsche-bahn-data
one row per train per stop, months of history"] L["DB Timetables + RIS::Stations
plan, live changes, cancellations, cause codes"] C["TimeNet connectors
error404/db-route-{week,quarter,season,multiscale}"] E["Trip examples
one train, one target stop, v7 features + XGBoost prior"] R --> C H --> C H --> E L --> E end subgraph Train["Training (Nebius H100 jobs)"] T1["Trip model
OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B, LoRA
split mode: history as time-series embeddings"] T2["Route model
OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B, LoRA
quarter profile: 60 days × 6 h"] E --> T1 C --> T2 end subgraph Serve["Serving"] S1["trip/serve.py :8502
Apple silicon MPS, live DB calls, 60 s cache"] S2["db_route/serve_route.py :8501
stored held-out forecasts + causes"] S3["db_route/serve_live.py on an H100
bucket relay via relay_proxy.py :8503"] T1 --> S1 T2 --> S2 T2 --> S3 end subgraph Backend["Node backend :8000 (zero dependencies)"] P["share-parser"] D["delay-prediction
PREDICT_URL → trip model
PREDICT_FALLBACK_URL → route model
connection chain"] A["recommendation · reroute"] W["causes ← CAUSES_URL"] J["training-jobs
submit / watch Nebius GPU jobs"] end subgraph App["React PWA (Vite, MapLibre)"] U["Plan · Map · My journey · What next? · Why? · Evidence"] end S1 --> D S3 --> D S2 --> W P --> U D --> U A --> U W --> U ``` **Three layers, one feature name per layer.** Every feature lives at `app//src/features//` on the frontend, the backend and the agents side, so `delay-prediction` in the app, the backend and the Python model server are the same feature in three halves. **Serving on one laptop.** The trip model runs on the Mac's GPU through MPS. The route model's stored forecasts and station causes are served from parquet and npz files with no torch at all. When a GPU job is up on Nebius, the route model also answers live per request: Nebius jobs have no inbound network, so requests travel as files through the project's storage bucket and the job answers the same way, about 0.6 s round trip plus 50 to 90 ms of inference. **The backend has no npm dependencies.** Node's built-in `http`, `fetch` and `crypto` are enough for parsing, chaining, the two model calls and the GPU job client. ## Data: sources and the agentic retrieval loop ### Sources All product data comes from Deutsche Bahn's official API Marketplace and from open datasets built from the same feeds. | Source | What we use it for | Coverage | |---|---|---| | [Timetables API](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/timetables) | Planned stops (`plan`), live delays, cancellations and platform changes (`fchg`), the route of every train | Current and upcoming trains; one key allows 60 calls per minute | | [RIS::Stations](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/ris-stations) | Official station names and EVA numbers | Current | | [`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data) (CC BY 4.0) | Stored Timetables responses, one row per train per stop, used for training | Months of history for all of Germany | | DB cause codes (IRIS) | Cause families per station for the "Why" tab and the cause-share series | From the same feeds | | Traveller question | DB data that answers it | |---|---| | "Which train and station is this?" | Timetables `station` lookup and RIS::Stations turn the share text into exact EVA station IDs | | "Is my train late right now?" | The change feed gives the current delay at every stop the train has passed | | "Will it get worse before my stop?" | Planned route and stops ahead, plus how earlier trains on the same line did today | | "Is this station having a bad day?" | Late share across all trains at the station in the last hours | | "Will this train be cancelled?" | Cancellation flags in the change feed, and how often this route was cancelled before | | "Will I make my change?" | Planned arrival and departure of both trains, combined with both delay distributions | ### The agentic retrieval loop Before any training, an agent decided which open time-series sources to use and how to map their columns onto our spec. It is a search, assess, select, retrieve and validate loop where **the LLM proposes and deterministic code disposes**: nothing the agent says is used until code has verified it. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["search
agent writes registry queries
code runs them live"] --> A["assess
agent rates relevance
code applies licence, credential,
coverage and cadence gates"] A --> P["select
agent fills a rubric
code probes the source live
(DuckDB over HTTP range reads)"] P --> M["retrieve
agent proposes a column map
code type-checks every column
against the probe"] M --> V["validate
accept/reject table with the
failing gate per source"] ``` | Step | The agent proposes | The code verifies or refuses | |---|---|---| | search | registry queries for four catalogues, from the data spec | every query runs against the live registry API | | assess | relevance of each candidate, with a reason | licence allow-list, credentials, coverage window, cadence, cheapest first | | select | rubric fields per surviving source | a live probe measures rows, columns, coverage and the station-basis step of 2 November 2025 | | retrieve | a column map from the source schema to the spec | every named column must exist and type-check against the probe, or the map is rejected | | validate | | `REJECTIONS.md` with the failing gate per source | An unverifiable proposal is dropped, never negotiated. Every LLM call, its prompt and its answer are logged so a reader can audit each decision. The loop also runs without an LLM: the same gates and probes, no proposals. **Run of record.** Window 2 November 2025 to 31 August 2026, four registries (a curated list, Hugging Face datasets, govdata CKAN, Zenodo): **354 candidates, 18 passed every gate, 7 probed live and used, 11 accepted on metadata only**. The rest are rejected with the gate that failed. The connectors that build the training datasets consume these decisions, not the loop's code. Why it matters for the model: what gets dropped is noise. Sources with the wrong cadence, an incompatible licence or a schema that does not type-check never reach the training set, so the model's inputs are only the columns the spec asked for and the probe confirmed. ## The two models and why we combine them Both models share one recipe: **Llama 3.2 3B** extended with **OpenTSLM** so it can read time series next to text, started from the published `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` checkpoint and fine-tuned with LoRA on Nebius H100s. Both answer with `Answer: ` or `Answer: cancelled`; instead of reading one number, we read the full softmax over the minute tokens, which gives a probability for every minute from 0 to 999 and the chance of cancellation. Training uses the exact minute plus a CRPS term so the distribution is calibrated, not just the median. ### Trip model: one train, one target stop, today - **Example:** a train heading to a stop. Inputs: the delays so far on this trip, this train number's usual gains along the line, the corridor's recent delays, how late the station is running, and the forecast of a statistical XGBoost model on the same features. - **Two prompt modes, both trained.** *Text* writes every series into the prompt as numbers. *Split* keeps the short trajectory in text and passes the long history, the same-train gains and the corridor series through the time-series encoder as embeddings. - **Live at request time.** The server fetches the train's current position from the Timetables API, assembles the same row the model was trained on, and forecasts. One key at 60 calls per minute serves about two new legs per minute; a cold four-train journey takes about a minute, repeats within a minute are instant. When DB live data fails, it answers with an offline estimate from recorded trips and says so. - **Explains itself.** The same model generates its rationale freely, about 360 tokens, so the app can show the model's own words next to the forecast. ### Route model: any recorded service, any station, any date - **Example:** a service group at a station on a travel date, with 60 days of six-hourly delay, throughput and cause-share history at that stop and across the service. Four profiles were trained in a bake-off (one week hourly, one quarter six-hourly, one season, multiscale); the **quarter** profile won every held-out cell. - **Covers what the trip model cannot.** 10,204 recorded service-station rows across 2,539 stations and 722 service groups, including trips days ahead for which the live timetable has nothing yet. It also carries the cause families per station that feed the "Why" tab. - **Served two ways:** from stored held-out forecasts on the laptop, or live per request on an H100 job through the bucket relay. ### Why combine them They fail in different places. The trip model is strongest for a train that is running now, because it reads its live position; for a journey next Tuesday it finds no trip and can only return the average of its train class. The route model knows every recorded service on the corridor regardless of the day, but nothing about today's position. So the backend asks the trip model first and hands only the legs it could not forecast to the route model. On a three-train journey two days out, that turned two "not a forecast" averages into model forecasts while keeping the live one. The ablation behind the presentation: text prompts alone, embeddings alone, and embeddings plus text. The results section states what each achieved; the embedding model is the one shipped in the app, the stacked text model at 12,000 steps is the submission checkpoint. ## Numbers Median error is the median absolute error of the predicted median in minutes; CRPS scores the whole distribution, lower is better. "Within a minute" is the share of trains whose predicted median is at most one minute off. ### Trip model against XGBoost on the same features | Test set | Trains | Model | XGBoost | Within a minute, model | Within a minute, XGBoost | |---|---:|---|---|---|---| | June to August, held out | 28,290 | 3.23 min | 3.30 min | 66% | 59% | | September, held out, forward in time | 9,573 | 2.53 min | 2.60 min | 70% | 62% | Shipped embedding model, split mode, 6,000 steps. The submitted stacked text model at 12,000 steps scores median error 3.19 / CRPS 2.54 on all 93,738 test examples and 2.52 / 1.99 on 10,000 September examples, beating XGBoost by 0.08 and 0.07 minutes with confidence intervals that exclude zero. ### Route model, quarter profile, 2,000 steps | Cell | Rows | Model | Gradient boosting | Persistence | Blend | |---|---:|---|---|---|---| | unseen trains and weeks (headline) | 462 | 1.82 / 1.37 | 1.82 / 1.37 | 1.84 | 1.79 / 1.35 | | known trains, unseen weeks (deployment) | 600 | 1.69 / 1.32 | 1.61 / 1.25 | 1.71 | 1.61 / 1.25 | Median error / CRPS in minutes. About 30% under the naive train-median baseline; 10 to 90% coverage 0.70 to 0.80 against a 0.80 target, so the distributions are slightly narrow. # delayedBahn — error404.ai Share your train trip from the DB app, and delayedBahn tells you how late each train is likely to be, whether you will make your change, and what to do about it. Two fine-tuned time-series language models, trained on Deutsche Bahn's own delay history, answer every trip you share. Built by team error404.ai at the European Hackathon League Zurich. ![Demo](docs/images/demo.png) ## Contents 1. [The problem](#the-problem) 2. [What we built](#what-we-built) 3. [Features, screen by screen](#features-screen-by-screen) 4. [How a shared trip flows through the system](#how-a-shared-trip-flows-through-the-system) 5. [Architecture](#architecture) 6. [Data: sources and the agentic retrieval loop](#data-sources-and-the-agentic-retrieval-loop) 7. [The two models and why we combine them](#the-two-models-and-why-we-combine-them) 8. [Numbers](#numbers) 9. [What is honest to say and what is not](#what-is-honest-to-say-and-what-is-not) 10. [Code structure](#code-structure) 11. [Quickstart](#quickstart) 12. [Team](#team) 13. [Built with](#built-with) 14. [Screenshots](#screenshots) --- ## The problem Deutsche Bahn runs about 40,000 trains a day, and every traveller knows the feeling: the planned journey looks fine on paper, then the first train arrives eleven minutes late and the change at Donauwörth is gone. The DB app shows the plan. It does not show the chance that the plan works. We cannot make the trains run on time. We can give travellers a reliable and comfortable journey anyway: know in advance which change is at risk, how much buffer would fix it, and which alternative to take if it fails. Three things make this hard, and shape everything below: - **Delays are uneven.** Most trains are a few minutes late, a few are very late. A single "expected delay" hides the risk; what a traveller needs is a distribution and the chance of the tight change. - **A journey is a chain.** It fails at its tightest connection. Per-train forecasts have to be chained across transfers. - **Data lives in many places.** Live positions from the DB API, months of history in open datasets, station cause codes, cancellations. Deciding what to fetch and what to drop is a task in itself. ## What we built - **Share a trip** from the DB app straight into our installable web app. It reads the trains, stations and times from the share text. - **A forecast per train:** likely arrival delay, a 10 to 90% range, the chance of arriving on time, and the chance of making each change, chained across the whole journey. - **Advice:** the plan is fine, add this much buffer, leave home by this time, or take one of these alternatives. If you already missed a change, the next connections from where you stand, each scored. - **The model's own words:** for every train, first the exact inputs the model read, then the explanation it writes itself. - **Why:** what usually goes wrong at each station, from DB's cause codes. - **Two models that complement each other:** a trip model that reads today's live train position, and a route model that knows every recorded service at every station. The backend asks the second whenever the first has nothing to go on. - **An agentic data retrieval loop** that searched four open-data registries, assessed 354 candidate sources, and kept the 7 that survived licence, coverage and live schema checks. Every decision is logged and auditable. ## Features, screen by screen | Screen | What it does | Backend call | |---|---|---| | **Plan** | Paste or share DB text. Drop a `.txt`. Try the example trip. Journey cards per train. | `POST /api/journeys/parse` | | **Map** | Your route on a satellite globe of Germany, legs coloured by risk, trains moving along the track, camera choreography per screen. | none | | **My journey** | Headline: the chance your plan fails. Per-train delay bars with range, chain strip across changes, a buffer slider that re-runs the chain on the client. Each train card carries the model's take: instantly the exact inputs it read, then its freely written explanation when ready, with a live "writing, train 2 of 3" note. | `POST /api/predict`, `POST /api/explain` | | **What next?** | Verdict and advice, leave-home-by time, alternatives compared, "I missed my connection" re-route list drawn on the map, share the result. | `POST /api/recommend`, `POST /api/reroute` | | **Why?** | Cause families at the station (works, weather, technical, knock-on), top DB cause codes, a 7-day sparkline. | `GET /api/causes` | | **Evidence** | Data sourcing, the model-versus-baseline chart, limitations, install button. | none | | **Install and share** | Installable PWA with a Web Share Target, so "Share" in DB Navigator lists delayedBahn. Stage mode for presenting from the app. | `GET /api/seed/demo` | Everything the app shows is labelled by where it came from: live forecast, recorded history, class average, or illustrative example. It never substitutes sample data for a real trip. ## How a shared trip flows through the system ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant DB as DB Navigator participant App as delayedBahn PWA participant BE as Node backend :8000 participant Trip as Trip model :8502
(Llama 3.2 3B + OpenTSLM, live DB data) participant Route as Route model :8501/:8503
(Llama 3.2 3B + OpenTSLM, 60-day history) participant DBAPI as DB Timetables API DB->>App: share text (Web Share Target /share?text=) App->>BE: POST /api/journeys/parse BE-->>App: Journey (trains, EVA stations, times) App->>BE: POST /api/predict BE->>Trip: forecast every leg Trip->>DBAPI: live position, stops ahead, station lateness Trip-->>BE: minute distribution per leg, or "class average" when no trip matches BE->>Route: forecast only the legs the trip model could not Route-->>BE: distribution from the recorded service at that station BE-->>App: chained forecast: per-train delay, change risk, plan-fail probability App->>BE: POST /api/recommend BE-->>App: verdict, buffer, alternatives loop one train at a time App->>BE: POST /api/explain BE->>Trip: generate the rationale in the model's own words Trip-->>App: two-sentence summary + full text end ``` 1. **Parse.** A grammar reads the DB share text in German or English (`RE16 (59129) … From 16:39 Nürnberg Hbf, Platform 5`) into trains, stations and times, and resolves stations to EVA numbers. 2. **Forecast.** The trip model gets every leg. For a train it can find in the live timetable it reads the delay so far, the stops ahead, how earlier trains on the line did today and how late the station is running, and answers with a probability for every minute from 0 to 999 plus the chance of cancellation. 3. **Complement.** For legs where the trip model has no recorded or live trip and would only return the average of its train class, the backend sends exactly those legs to the route model, which forecasts the recorded service at that station from 60 days of six-hourly history. The reply names both models and marks which legs came from which. 4. **Chain.** The change probability at each transfer comes from the two trains' distributions and the planned transfer time; the plan-fail probability chains all changes. This is a JavaScript port of the Python `connection.py`, so the buffer slider can re-run it on the client. 5. **Advise.** The recommendation feature turns the chain into a verdict, a leave-home-by time, and scored alternatives. 6. **Explain.** After the forecast, the app asks for each train's explanation in turn. LLM proposes, code verifies"] H["piebro/deutsche-bahn-data
one row per train per stop, months of history"] L["DB Timetables + RIS::Stations
plan, live changes, cancellations, cause codes"] C["TimeNet connectors
error404/db-route-{week,quarter,season,multiscale}"] E["Trip examples
one train, one target stop, v7 features + XGBoost prior"] R --> C H --> C H --> E L --> E end subgraph Train["Training (Nebius H100 jobs)"] T1["Trip model
OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B, LoRA
split mode: history as time-series embeddings"] T2["Route model
OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B, LoRA
quarter profile: 60 days × 6 h"] E --> T1 C --> T2 end subgraph Serve["Serving"] S1["trip/serve.py :8502
Apple silicon MPS, live DB calls, 60 s cache"] S2["db_route/serve_route.py :8501
stored held-out forecasts + causes"] S3["db_route/serve_live.py on an H100
bucket relay via relay_proxy.py :8503"] T1 --> S1 T2 --> S2 T2 --> S3 end subgraph Backend["Node backend :8000 (zero dependencies)"] P["share-parser"] D["delay-prediction
PREDICT_URL → trip model
PREDICT_FALLBACK_URL → route model
connection chain"] A["recommendation · reroute"] W["causes ← CAUSES_URL"] J["training-jobs
submit / watch Nebius GPU jobs"] end subgraph App["React PWA (Vite, MapLibre)"] U["Plan · Map · My journey · What next? · Why? · Evidence"] end S1 --> D S3 --> D S2 --> W P --> U D --> U A --> U W --> U ``` **Three layers, one feature name per layer.** Every feature lives at `app//src/features//` on the frontend, the backend and the agents side, so `delay-prediction` in the app, the backend and the Python model server are the same feature in three halves. **Serving on one laptop.** The trip model runs on the Mac's GPU through MPS. The route model's stored forecasts and station causes are served from parquet and npz files with no torch at all. When a GPU job is up on Nebius, the route model also answers live per request: Nebius jobs have no inbound network, so requests travel as files through the project's storage bucket and the job answers the same way, about 0.6 s round trip plus 50 to 90 ms of inference. **The backend has no npm dependencies.** Node's built-in `http`, `fetch` and `crypto` are enough for parsing, chaining, the two model calls and the GPU job client. ## Data: sources and the agentic retrieval loop ### Sources All product data comes from Deutsche Bahn's official API Marketplace and from open datasets built from the same feeds. | Source | What we use it for | Coverage | |---|---|---| | [Timetables API](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/timetables) | Planned stops (`plan`), live delays, cancellations and platform changes (`fchg`), the route of every train | Current and upcoming trains; one key allows 60 calls per minute | | [RIS::Stations](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/ris-stations) | Official station names and EVA numbers | Current | | [`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data) (CC BY 4.0) | Stored Timetables responses, one row per train per stop, used for training | Months of history for all of Germany | | DB cause codes (IRIS) | Cause families per station for the "Why" tab and the cause-share series | From the same feeds | | Traveller question | DB data that answers it | |---|---| | "Which train and station is this?" | Timetables `station` lookup and RIS::Stations turn the share text into exact EVA station IDs | | "Is my train late right now?" | The change feed gives the current delay at every stop the train has passed | | "Will it get worse before my stop?" | Planned route and stops ahead, plus how earlier trains on the same line did today | | "Is this station having a bad day?" | Late share across all trains at the station in the last hours | | "Will this train be cancelled?" | Cancellation flags in the change feed, and how often this route was cancelled before | | "Will I make my change?" | Planned arrival and departure of both trains, combined with both delay distributions | ### The agentic retrieval loop Before any training, an agent decided which open time-series sources to use and how to map their columns onto our spec. It is a search, assess, select, retrieve and validate loop where **the LLM proposes and deterministic code disposes**: nothing the agent says is used until code has verified it. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["search
agent writes registry queries
code runs them live"] --> A["assess
agent rates relevance
code applies licence, credential,
coverage and cadence gates"] A --> P["select
agent fills a rubric
code probes the source live
(DuckDB over HTTP range reads)"] P --> M["retrieve

against the probe"] M --> V["validate

failing gate per source"] ``` | Step | The agent proposes | The code verifies or refuses | |---|---|---| | search | registry queries for four catalogues, from the data spec | every query runs against the live registry API | | assess | relevance of each candidate, with a reason | licence allow-list, credentials, coverage window, cadence, cheapest first | | select | rubric fields per surviving source | a live probe measures rows, columns, coverage and the station-basis step of 2 November 2025 | | retrieve | a column map from the source schema to the spec | every named column must exist and type-check against the probe, or the map is rejected | | validate | | `REJECTIONS.md` with the failing gate per source | An unverifiable proposal is dropped, never negotiated. Every LLM call, its prompt and its answer are logged so a reader can audit each decision. The loop also runs without an LLM: the same gates and probes, no proposals. **Run of record.** Window 2 November 2025 to 31 August 2026, four registries (a curated list, Hugging Face datasets, govdata CKAN, Zenodo): **354 candidates, 18 passed every gate, 7 probed live and used, 11 accepted on metadata only**. The rest are rejected with the gate that failed. The connectors that build the training datasets consume these decisions, not the loop's code. Why it matters for the model: what gets dropped is noise. Sources with the wrong cadence, an incompatible licence or a schema that does not type-check never reach the training set, so the model's inputs are only the columns the spec asked for and the probe confirmed. ## The two models and why we combine them Both models share one recipe: **Llama 3.2 3B** extended with **OpenTSLM** so it can read time series next to text, started from the published `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` checkpoint and fine-tuned with LoRA on Nebius H100s. Both answer with `Answer: ` or `Answer: cancelled`; instead of reading one number, we read the full softmax over the minute tokens, which gives a probability for every minute from 0 to 999 and the chance of cancellation. Training uses the exact minute plus a CRPS term so the distribution is calibrated, not just the median. ### Trip model: one train, one target stop, today - **Example:** a train heading to a stop. Inputs: the delays so far on this trip, this train number's usual gains along the line, the corridor's recent delays, how late the station is running, and the forecast of a statistical XGBoost model on the same features. - **Two prompt modes, both trained.** *Text* writes every series into the prompt as numbers. *Split* keeps the short trajectory in text and passes the long history, the same-train gains and the corridor series through the time-series encoder as embeddings. - **Live at request time.** The server fetches the train's current position from the Timetables API, assembles the same row the model was trained on, and forecasts. One key at 60 calls per minute serves about two new legs per minute; a cold four-train journey takes about a minute, repeats within a minute are instant. The route model knows every recorded service on the corridor regardless of the day, but nothing about today's position. # delayedBahn — error404.ai Share your train trip from the DB app, and delayedBahn tells you how late each train is likely to be, whether you will make your change, and what to do about it. Two fine-tuned time-series language models, trained on Deutsche Bahn's own delay history, answer every trip you share. Built by team error404.ai at the European Hackathon League Zurich. ![Demo](docs/images/demo.png) ## Contents 1. [The problem](#the-problem) 2. [What we built](#what-we-built) 3. [Features, screen by screen](#features-screen-by-screen) 4. [How a shared trip flows through the system](#how-a-shared-trip-flows-through-the-system) 5. [Architecture](#architecture) 6. [Data: sources and the agentic retrieval loop](#data-sources-and-the-agentic-retrieval-loop) 7. [The two models and why we combine them](#the-two-models-and-why-we-combine-them) 8. [Numbers](#numbers) 9. [What is honest to say and what is not](#what-is-honest-to-say-and-what-is-not) 10. [Code structure](#code-structure) 11. [Quickstart](#quickstart) 12. [Team](#team) 13. [Built with](#built-with) 14. [Screenshots](#screenshots) --- ## The problem Deutsche Bahn runs about 40,000 trains a day, and every traveller knows the feeling: the planned journey looks fine on paper, then the first train arrives eleven minutes late and the change at Donauwörth is gone. The DB app shows the plan. It does not show the chance that the plan works. We cannot make the trains run on time. We can give travellers a reliable and comfortable journey anyway: know in advance which change is at risk, how much buffer would fix it, and which alternative to take if it fails. Three things make this hard, and shape everything below: - **Delays are uneven.** Most trains are a few minutes late, a few are very late. A single "expected delay" hides the risk; what a traveller needs is a distribution and the chance of the tight change. - **A journey is a chain.** It fails at its tightest connection. Per-train forecasts have to be chained across transfers. - **Data lives in many places.** Live positions from the DB API, months of history in open datasets, station cause codes, cancellations. Deciding what to fetch and what to drop is a task in itself. ## What we built - **Share a trip** from the DB app straight into our installable web app. It reads the trains, stations and times from the share text. - **A forecast per train:** likely arrival delay, a 10 to 90% range, the chance of arriving on time, and the chance of making each change, chained across the whole journey. - **Advice:** the plan is fine, add this much buffer, leave home by this time, or take one of these alternatives. If you already missed a change, the next connections from where you stand, each scored. - **The model's own words:** for every train, first the exact inputs the model read, then the explanation it writes itself. - **Why:** what usually goes wrong at each station, from DB's cause codes. - **Two models that complement each other:** a trip model that reads today's live train position, and a route model that knows every recorded service at every station. The backend asks the second whenever the first has nothing to go on. - **An agentic data retrieval loop** that searched four open-data registries, assessed 354 candidate sources, and kept the 7 that survived licence, coverage and live schema checks. Every decision is logged and auditable. ## Features, screen by screen | Screen | What it does | Backend call | |---|---|---| | **Plan** | Paste or share DB text. Drop a `.txt`. Try the example trip. Journey cards per train. | `POST /api/journeys/parse` | | **Map** | Your route on a satellite globe of Germany, legs coloured by risk, trains moving along the track, camera choreography per screen. | none | | **My journey** | Headline: the chance your plan fails. Per-train delay bars with range, chain strip across changes, a buffer slider that re-runs the chain on the client. Each train card carries the model's take: instantly the exact inputs it read, then its freely written explanation when ready, with a live "writing, train 2 of 3" note. | `POST /api/predict`, `POST /api/explain` | | **What next?** | Verdict and advice, leave-home-by time, alternatives compared, "I missed my connection" re-route list drawn on the map, share the result. | `POST /api/recommend`, `POST /api/reroute` | | **Why?** | Cause families at the station (works, weather, technical, knock-on), top DB cause codes, a 7-day sparkline. | `GET /api/causes` | | **Evidence** | Data sourcing, the model-versus-baseline chart, limitations, install button. | none | | **Install and share** | Installable PWA with a Web Share Target, so "Share" in DB Navigator lists delayedBahn. Stage mode for presenting from the app. | `GET /api/seed/demo` | Everything the app shows is labelled by where it came from: live forecast, recorded history, class average, or illustrative example. It never substitutes sample data for a real trip. ## How a shared trip flows through the system ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant DB as DB Navigator participant App as delayedBahn PWA participant BE as Node backend :8000 participant Trip as Trip model :8502
(Llama 3.2 3B + OpenTSLM, live DB data) participant Route as Route model :8501/:8503
(Llama 3.2 3B + OpenTSLM, 60-day history) participant DBAPI as DB Timetables API DB->>App: share text (Web Share Target /share?text=) App->>BE: POST /api/journeys/parse BE-->>App: Journey (trains, EVA stations, times) App->>BE: POST /api/predict BE->>Trip: forecast every leg Trip->>DBAPI: live position, stops ahead, station lateness Trip-->>BE: minute distribution per leg, or "class average" when no trip matches BE->>Route: forecast only the legs the trip model could not Route-->>BE: distribution from the recorded service at that station BE-->>App: chained forecast: per-train delay, change risk, plan-fail probability App->>BE: POST /api/recommend BE-->>App: verdict, buffer, alternatives loop one train at a time App->>BE: POST /api/explain BE->>Trip: generate the rationale in the model's own words Trip-->>App: two-sentence summary + full text end ``` 1. **Parse.** A grammar reads the DB share text in German or English (`RE16 (59129) … From 16:39 Nürnberg Hbf, Platform 5`) into trains, stations and times, and resolves stations to EVA numbers. 2. **Forecast.** The trip model gets every leg. For a train it can find in the live timetable it reads the delay so far, the stops ahead, how earlier trains on the line did today and how late the station is running, and answers with a probability for every minute from 0 to 999 plus the chance of cancellation. 3. **Complement.** For legs where the trip model has no recorded or live trip and would only return the average of its train class, the backend sends exactly those legs to the route model, which forecasts the recorded service at that station from 60 days of six-hourly history. The reply names both models and marks which legs came from which. 4. **Chain.** The change probability at each transfer comes from the two trains' distributions and the planned transfer time; the plan-fail probability chains all changes. This is a JavaScript port of the Python `connection.py`, so the buffer slider can re-run it on the client. 5. **Advise.** The recommendation feature turns the chain into a verdict, a leave-home-by time, and scored alternatives. 6. **Explain.** After the forecast, the app asks for each train's explanation in turn. Generation is slow on a laptop, about a minute per train, so the card shows the instant rationale first and swaps in the model's own words when they arrive. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Data["Data layer (Python, app/agents)"] R["Agentic retrieval loop
search · assess · select · retrieve · validate
LLM proposes, code verifies"] H["piebro/deutsche-bahn-data
one row per train per stop, months of history"] L["DB Timetables + RIS::Stations
plan, live changes, cancellations, cause codes"] C["TimeNet connectors
error404/db-route-{week,quarter,season,multiscale}"] E["Trip examples
one train, one target stop, v7 features + XGBoost prior"] R --> C H --> C H --> E L --> E end subgraph Train["Training (Nebius H100 jobs)"] T1["Trip model
OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B, LoRA
split mode: history as time-series embeddings"] T2["Route model
OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B, LoRA
quarter profile: 60 days × 6 h"] E --> T1 C --> T2 end subgraph Serve["Serving"] S1["trip/serve.py :8502
Apple silicon MPS, live DB calls, 60 s cache"] S2["db_route/serve_route.py :8501
stored held-out forecasts + causes"] S3["db_route/serve_live.py on an H100
bucket relay via relay_proxy.py :8503"] T1 --> S1 T2 --> S2 T2 --> S3 end subgraph Backend["Node backend :8000 (zero dependencies)"] P["share-parser"] D["delay-prediction
PREDICT_URL → trip model
PREDICT_FALLBACK_URL → route model
connection chain"] A["recommendation · reroute"] W["causes ← CAUSES_URL"] J["training-jobs
submit / watch Nebius GPU jobs"] end subgraph App["React PWA (Vite, MapLibre)"] U["Plan · Map · My journey · What next? · Why? · Evidence"] end S1 --> D S3 --> D S2 --> W P --> U D --> U A --> U W --> U ``` **Three layers, one feature name per layer.** Every feature lives at `app//src/features//` on the frontend, the backend and the agents side, so `delay-prediction` in the app, the backend and the Python model server are the same feature in three halves. **Serving on one laptop.** The trip model runs on the Mac's GPU through MPS. The route model's stored forecasts and station causes are served from parquet and npz files with no torch at all. When a GPU job is up on Nebius, the route model also answers live per request: Nebius jobs have no inbound network, so requests travel as files through the project's storage bucket and the job answers the same way, about 0.6 s round trip plus 50 to 90 ms of inference. **The backend has no npm dependencies.** Node's built-in `http`, `fetch` and `crypto` are enough for parsing, chaining, the two model calls and the GPU job client. ## Data: sources and the agentic retrieval loop ### Sources All product data comes from Deutsche Bahn's official API Marketplace and from open datasets built from the same feeds. | Source | What we use it for | Coverage | |---|---|---| | [Timetables API](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/timetables) | Planned stops (`plan`), live delays, cancellations and platform changes (`fchg`), the route of every train | Current and upcoming trains; one key allows 60 calls per minute | | [RIS::Stations](https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/ris-stations) | Official station names and EVA numbers | Current | | [`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data) (CC BY 4.0) | Stored Timetables responses, one row per train per stop, used for training | Months of history for all of Germany | | DB cause codes (IRIS) | Cause families per station for the "Why" tab and the cause-share series | From the same feeds | | Traveller question | DB data that answers it | |---|---| | "Which train and station is this?" | Timetables `station` lookup and RIS::Stations turn the share text into exact EVA station IDs | | "Is my train late right now?" | The change feed gives the current delay at every stop the train has passed | | "Will it get worse before my stop?" | Planned route and stops ahead, plus how earlier trains on the same line did today | | "Is this station having a bad day?" | Late share across all trains at the station in the last hours | | "Will this train be cancelled?" | Cancellation flags in the change feed, and how often this route was cancelled before | | "Will I make my change?" | Planned arrival and departure of both trains, combined with both delay distributions | ### The agentic retrieval loop Before any training, an agent decided which open time-series sources to use and how to map their columns onto our spec. It is a search, assess, select, retrieve and validate loop where **the LLM proposes and deterministic code disposes**: nothing the agent says is used until code has verified it. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["search
agent writes registry queries
code runs them live"] --> A["assess
agent rates relevance
code applies licence, credential,
coverage and cadence gates"] A --> P["select
agent fills a rubric
code probes the source live
(DuckDB over HTTP range reads)"] P --> M["retrieve
agent proposes a column map
code type-checks every column
against the probe"] M --> V["validate
accept/reject table with the
failing gate per source"] ``` | Step | The agent proposes | The code verifies or refuses | |---|---|---| | search | registry queries for four catalogues, from the data spec | every query runs against the live registry API | | assess | relevance of each candidate, with a reason | licence allow-list, credentials, coverage window, cadence, cheapest first | | select | rubric fields per surviving source | a live probe measures rows, columns, coverage and the station-basis step of 2 November 2025 | | retrieve | a column map from the source schema to the spec | every named column must exist and type-check against the probe, or the map is rejected | | validate | | `REJECTIONS.md` with the failing gate per source | An unverifiable proposal is dropped, never negotiated. Every LLM call, its prompt and its answer are logged so a reader can audit each decision. The loop also runs without an LLM: the same gates and probes, no proposals. **Run of record.** Window 2 November 2025 to 31 August 2026, four registries (a curated list, Hugging Face datasets, govdata CKAN, Zenodo): **354 candidates, 18 passed every gate, 7 probed live and used, 11 accepted on metadata only**. The rest are rejected with the gate that failed. The connectors that build the training datasets consume these decisions, not the loop's code. Why it matters for the model: what gets dropped is noise. Sources with the wrong cadence, an incompatible licence or a schema that does not type-check never reach the training set, so the model's inputs are only the columns the spec asked for and the probe confirmed. ## The two models and why we combine them Both models share one recipe: **Llama 3.2 3B** extended with **OpenTSLM** so it can read time series next to text, started from the published `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` checkpoint and fine-tuned with LoRA on Nebius H100s. Both answer with `Answer: ` or `Answer: cancelled`; instead of reading one number, we read the full softmax over the minute tokens, which gives a probability for every minute from 0 to 999 and the chance of cancellation. Training uses the exact minute plus a CRPS term so the distribution is calibrated, not just the median. ### Trip model: one train, one target stop, today - **Example:** a train heading to a stop. Inputs: the delays so far on this trip, this train number's usual gains along the line, the corridor's recent delays, how late the station is running, and the forecast of a statistical XGBoost model on the same features. - **Two prompt modes, both trained.** *Text* writes every series into the prompt as numbers. *Split* keeps the short trajectory in text and passes the long history, the same-train gains and the corridor series through the time-series encoder as embeddings. - **Live at request time.** The server fetches the train's current position from the Timetables API, assembles the same row the model was trained on, and forecasts. One key at 60 calls per minute serves about two new legs per minute; a cold four-train journey takes about a minute, repeats within a minute are instant. When DB live data fails, it answers with an offline estimate from recorded trips and says so. - **Explains itself.** The same model generates its rationale freely, about 360 tokens, so the app can show the model's own words next to the forecast. ### Route model: any recorded service, any station, any date - **Example:** a service group at a station on a travel date, with 60 days of six-hourly delay, throughput and cause-share history at that stop and across the service. Four profiles were trained in a bake-off (one week hourly, one quarter six-hourly, one season, multiscale); the **quarter** profile won every held-out cell. - **Covers what the trip model cannot.** 10,204 recorded service-station rows across 2,539 stations and 722 service groups, including trips days ahead for which the live timetable has nothing yet. It also carries the cause families per station that feed the "Why" tab. - **Served two ways:** from stored held-out forecasts on the laptop, or live per request on an H100 job through the bucket relay. ### Why combine them They fail in different places. The trip model is strongest for a train that is running now, because it reads its live position; for a journey next Tuesday it finds no trip and can only return the average of its train class. The route model knows every recorded service on the corridor regardless of the day, but nothing about today's position. So the backend asks the trip model first and hands only the legs it could not forecast to the route model. On a three-train journey two days out, that turned two "not a forecast" averages into model forecasts while keeping the live one. The ablation behind the presentation: text prompts alone, embeddings alone, and embeddings plus text. The results section states what each achieved; the embedding model is the one shipped in the app, the stacked text model at 12,000 steps is the submission checkpoint. ## Numbers Median error is the median absolute error of the predicted median in minutes; CRPS scores the whole distribution, lower is better. "Within a minute" is the share of trains whose predicted median is at most one minute off. ### Trip model against XGBoost on the same features | Test set | Trains | Model | XGBoost | Within a minute, model | Within a minute, XGBoost | |---|---:|---|---|---|---| | June to August, held out | 28,290 | 3.23 min | 3.30 min | 66% | 59% | | September, held out, forward in time | 9,573 | 2.53 min | 2.60 min | 70% | 62% | Shipped embedding model, split mode, 6,000 steps. The submitted stacked text model at 12,000 steps scores median error 3.19 / CRPS 2.54 on all 93,738 test examples and 2.52 / 1.99 on 10,000 September examples, beating XGBoost by 0.08 and 0.07 minutes with confidence intervals that exclude zero. ### Route model, quarter profile, 2,000 steps | Cell | Rows | Model | Gradient boosting | Persistence | Blend | |---|---:|---|---|---|---| | unseen trains and weeks (headline) | 462 | 1.82 / 1.37 | 1.82 / 1.37 | 1.84 | 1.79 / 1.35 | | known trains, unseen weeks (deployment) | 600 | 1.69 / 1.32 | 1.61 / 1.25 | 1.71 | 1.61 / 1.25 | Median error / CRPS in minutes. About 30% under the naive train-median baseline; 10 to 90% coverage 0.70 to 0.80 against a 0.80 target, so the distributions are slightly narrow. Generated-answer accuracy on late/on-time plus cause family: 0.73 against a 0.38 majority class. ### Retrieval loop 354 candidate sources, 18 passed every gate, 7 probed and used, every rejection recorded with its failing gate. ### Serving | | | |---|---| | Trip model, cached leg | milliseconds | | Trip model, cold leg with live DB data | 15 to 40 API calls, up to a minute at 60 calls per minute | | Route model, stored forecast | 7 ms for a whole journey | | Route model, live on the H100 through the bucket relay | 0.6 s round trip, 50 to 90 ms of inference | | The model's own explanation | about a minute per train on a laptop | ## What is honest to say and what is not - **The models beat a strong tabular baseline by a small, consistent margin.** Tenths of a minute, with confidence intervals that exclude zero on the trip model. They are not an order of magnitude better than XGBoost, and we say so on the Evidence screen. - **A forecast for a day ahead is a forecast of the recorded service, not of that train.** The route model's reply names the record, its travel date and what then happened; the app labels it. - **The model's own words can misstate numbers.** They are generated freely; the estimate above them reads the exact inputs. +Why it matters for the model: what gets dropped is noise. Sources with the wrong cadence, an incompatible licence or a schema that does not type-check never reach the training set, so the model's inputs are only the columns the spec asked for and the probe confirmed.

+Both models share one recipe: **Llama 3.2 3B** extended with **OpenTSLM** so it can read time series next to text, started from the published `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` checkpoint and fine-tuned with LoRA on Nebius H100s. Both answer with `Answer: <minutes>` or `Answer: cancelled`; instead of reading one number, we read the full softmax over the minute tokens, which gives a probability for every minute from 0 to 999 and the chance of cancellation. Training uses the exact minute plus a CRPS term so the distribution is calibrated, not just the median.
+### Trip model: one train, one target stop, today

+- **Example:** a train heading to a stop. Inputs: the delays so far on this trip, this train number's usual gains along the line, the corridor's recent delays, how late the station is running, and the forecast of a statistical XGBoost model on the same features.

+- **Two prompt modes, both trained.** *Text* writes every series into the prompt as numbers. *Split* keeps the short trajectory in text and passes the long history, the same-train gains and the corridor series through the time-series encoder as embeddings.

+- **Live at request time.** The server fetches the train's current position from the Timetables API, assembles the same row the model was trained on, and forecasts. One key at 60 calls per minute serves about two new legs per minute; a cold four-train journey takes about a minute, repeats within a minute are instant. When DB live data fails, it answers with an offline estimate from recorded trips and says so.
+- **Explains itself.** The same model generates its rationale freely, about 360 tokens, so the app can show the model's own words next to the forecast.
+### Route model: any recorded service, any station, any date

+- **Example:** a service group at a station on a travel date, with 60 days of six-hourly delay, throughput and cause-share history at that stop and across the service. Four profiles were trained in a bake-off (one week hourly, one quarter six-hourly, one season, multiscale); the **quarter** profile won every held-out cell.

+They fail in different places. The trip model is strongest for a train that is running now, because it reads its live position; for a journey next Tuesday it finds no trip and can only return the average of its train class. The route model knows every recorded service on the corridor regardless of the day, but nothing about today's position. So the backend asks the trip model first and hands only the legs it could not forecast to the route model. On a three-train journey two days out, that turned two "not a forecast" averages into model forecasts while keeping the live one.

+The ablation behind the presentation: text prompts alone, embeddings alone, and embeddings plus text. The results section states what each achieved; the embedding model is the one shipped in the app, the stacked text model at 12,000 steps is the submission checkpoint.

+Median error is the median absolute error of the predicted median in minutes; CRPS scores the whole distribution, lower is better. "Within a minute" is the share of trains whose predicted median is at most one minute off.

+- **A forecast for a day ahead is a forecast of the recorded service, not of that train.** The route model's reply names the record, its travel date and what then happened; the app labels it.

+- **Live data is rate-limited.** One DB key means the first check of a long journey takes about a minute. The app shows progress rather than a spinner.
+- **Nothing is substituted.** When a service is down the app says which one, and only the bundled example trip ever falls back to a bundled sample, labelled as such.

The README is rewritten around the story from the transcript, with diagrams in place of the screenshots you will add. It is 360 lines, uncommitted, on top of Yash's version.

**What it now covers, in order**

1. **The problem** as the pitch opens: DB delays happen, we can't fix the trains, we can give travellers a reliable journey. The three things that make it hard: uneven delays, journeys as chains, data in many places.
2. **What we built** and a **screen-by-screen feature table** with the backend call behind each screen.
3. **The flow** as a sequence diagram: share from DB, parse, trip model with live DB data, route model for the legs it can't cover, chaining, advice, then the model's own words one train at a time.
4. **Architecture** as a layered diagram: agentic retrieval and data sources, the two training runs on Nebius, the three serving paths, the zero-dependency backend, the PWA.
5. **Data sources** and the **agentic retrieval loop** with its own diagram and the proposer-verifier table: the LLM proposes, code verifies, unverifiable proposals are dropped. Run of record: 354 candidates, 18 passed the gates, 7 used. It also says why this matters for the model: dropped sources are dropped noise.
6. **The two models and why we combine them**, including the text versus embeddings ablation, which is the shipped model and which is the submission.
7. **Numbers** in tables: trip model versus XGBoost on both test sets, route model per cell against gradient boosting and persistence, retrieval counts, serving latencies.
8. **What is honest to say and what is not**, since the transcript asked for full honesty: small consistent margins over XGBoost, day-ahead forecasts are of the recorded service, generated text can misstate numbers, live data is rate-limited, nothing is substituted.
9. Code structure, quickstart with the combined-models start, team, built with, and the existing screenshot placeholders untouched.

**Two things to check before you present**

- **Team roles** in the Team section are my reading of who owned which branch. Adjust the wording if it is off.
- **Jonas's numbers at 10:30** from the transcript: I used what is in his README and the zip's instructions. If he has newer figures for the embeddings versus text comparison, the Numbers section is where they go.

Nothing is pushed. GitHub main matches your local main except for today's uncommitted work, which is now 19 files including this README and the combined-model backend. Say the word and I will commit and push it.
